I will keep my land in the standard Quzhou pattern of `winter wheat + summer maize` double cropping. I am in southern Hebei on the North China Plain, so this is still the most reliable use of land, machinery, labor, and irrigation water for me. At the start of this season, the winter wheat is already the main crop standing in the field, and I will carry it through harvest, then turn the same land quickly into summer maize. I will not split much area into specialty crops, because I would rather protect yield stability, keep field operations simple, and avoid adding marketing risk.

For wheat, I will stay with an improved winter wheat variety instead of older traditional seed, because I want stable yield, lodging resistance, and better disease tolerance. I will manage fertilizer more carefully than a rough “more is better” approach: enough nitrogen to support yield, but with phosphorus and potassium kept in balance so the crop stands well and fills grain properly. I will use rotary tillage ahead of wheat establishment and then focus on a few key irrigations, because water matters a lot here and I do not want to over-irrigate. I will keep pesticide use targeted, mainly for weeds and the main disease/insect pressure windows, rather than spraying excessively.

For summer maize, I will use a hybrid, because that is the clear yield choice for me after wheat harvest. I will sow quickly after the wheat comes off so I do not lose heat or moisture. I will keep tillage light and practical, using rotary tillage to turn the field around fast. I will apply nitrogen more heavily to maize than wheat, but still with phosphorus and potassium included so the crop does not run out during grain filling. I will plan fewer irrigations than wheat unless the season turns dry, and I will keep pesticide applications limited to the pressure I actually see in the field. My whole strategy is simple: stable double cropping, improved seed, balanced fertilizer, controlled water use, and no unnecessary complexity.
